metadata.file_name: 133. Xie et al. (2023). Effects of Teacher Collaboration on Teaching Practices in China and England: A Structural Equation Model With TALIS 2018 Data.pdf
metadata.title: Effects of Teacher Collaboration on Teaching Practices in China and England: A Structural Equation Model With TALIS 2018 Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data with a two-stage sampling design: schools were sampled within region-based groups, and then 20 teachers were sampled per school (or all qualified teachers if fewer than 20). The manuscript describes the sampling procedure for representativeness but does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme in the SEM estimation. Because the analysis is based on confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling in Mplus (maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors), the paper does not specify a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) for complex-survey correction. Therefore, readers should treat the results as model-based associations from the sampled teacher data unless the authors’ TALIS weight handling is confirmed elsewhere (it is not documented in the provided text).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study models latent constructs from TALIS questionnaire items using CFA/SEM rather than cognitive achievement scores with plausible values. As a result, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the dependent variables (teaching practices, teacher collaboration, and teacher self-efficacy). The manuscript does not report any missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, FIML, or multiple imputation), which is a reporting gap because SEM results can be sensitive to how missing questionnaire responses are handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teachers from China and England/UK, drawn using TALIS’s two-stage sampling design (randomly selected schools within region-based groups, then random selection of 20 teachers per school, or all qualified teachers if fewer than 20). The paper restricts the scope to lower-secondary teachers and uses the TALIS questionnaire constructs for teacher collaboration (COLES, EXCH), teacher self-efficacy (SELF composite from three subscales), and teaching practices (TP with CLAIN, COGAC, ASS). No additional exclusion criteria (e.g., item nonresponse thresholds) are explicitly described in the provided text.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: EXCH→CLAIN b=0.206 (p<.01); COLES→CLAIN b=2.006 (p>.05, non-significant). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.109 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.064, 0.161]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China, the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination (EXCH) and teacher self-efficacy (SELF) to model clarity of instruction (CLAIN), finding that EXCH had a positive direct association with clarity of instruction while professional collaboration (COLES) was not directly significant. The mediation results further showed that professional collaboration had significant indirect effects on clarity of instruction through teacher self-efficacy. This indicates that strengthening teacher self-efficacy may be a key mechanism through which certain collaboration forms translate into clearer instructional communication, though the study is correlational and SEM mediation does not establish causality.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: COLES→COGAC b=0.080 (p>.05, non-significant); EXCH→COGAC b=0.067 (p>.05, non-significant). SELF→COGAC b=0.341 (p<.001). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.093 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.053, 0.138]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China, the study leveraged teacher self-efficacy (SELF) and collaboration constructs to predict cognitive activation (COGAC), finding that SELF had a strong positive direct effect while both professional collaboration (COLES) and exchange/co-ordination (EXCH) were not directly significant. Mediation analysis showed that professional collaboration influenced cognitive activation indirectly through teacher self-efficacy, whereas exchange/co-ordination did not show an indirect effect via SELF. This indicates that policies aiming to raise teachers’ efficacy beliefs may be more effective for promoting higher-order, student-centered cognitive activation than relying on collaboration forms alone, though causal claims cannot be inferred from cross-sectional SEM.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: EXCH→ASS b=0.261 (p<.01); COLES→ASS b=0.020 (p>.05, non-significant). SELF→ASS b=0.426 (p<.001). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.166 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.068, 0.173]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China, the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination (EXCH) and teacher self-efficacy (SELF) to predict classroom assessment (ASS), finding that EXCH had a positive direct association with classroom assessment while professional collaboration (COLES) was not directly significant. The mediation results showed that professional collaboration had significant indirect effects on classroom assessment through teacher self-efficacy, whereas exchange/co-ordination did not. This indicates that improving teacher self-efficacy can help collaboration translate into more formative assessment practices, suggesting teacher development programs should pair collaboration opportunities with efficacy-building supports, while recognizing the correlational nature of the evidence.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: COLES→CLAIN b=0.044 (p>.05, non-significant); EXCH→CLAIN b=0.118 (p<.05). SELF→CLAIN b=0.553 (p<.001). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.132 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.071, 0.193]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for England/UK, the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination (EXCH) and teacher self-efficacy (SELF) to model clarity of instruction (CLAIN), finding that EXCH had a positive direct association while professional collaboration (COLES) was not directly significant. Mediation analysis showed that professional collaboration affected clarity of instruction indirectly through teacher self-efficacy, whereas exchange/co-ordination did not show an indirect effect via SELF. This indicates that collaboration mechanisms that support teachers’ efficacy beliefs may be important for improving instructional clarity, implying that teacher professional development should explicitly cultivate self-efficacy alongside collaboration structures, while noting that SEM mediation does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: COLES→COGAC b=0.406 (p<.001); EXCH→COGAC b=-2.173 (p<.01, negative); SELF→COGAC b=0.437 (p<.001). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.104 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.058, 0.145]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for England/UK, the study leveraged professional collaboration (COLES), exchange/co-ordination (EXCH), and teacher self-efficacy (SELF) to predict cognitive activation (COGAC), finding that professional collaboration had a positive direct effect while exchange/co-ordination had a negative direct effect. The mediation results further showed that professional collaboration influenced cognitive activation indirectly through teacher self-efficacy, whereas exchange/co-ordination did not. This indicates that not all collaboration forms are equally beneficial for promoting higher-order, student-centered cognitive activation; professional collaboration may need to be prioritized and paired with efficacy supports to avoid unintended negative associations, though causality cannot be concluded from cross-sectional SEM.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (Mplus ML with robust standard errors). Direct effects: COLES→ASS b=0.152 (p<.05); EXCH→ASS b=0.073 (p>.05, non-significant). SELF→ASS b=0.325 (p<.001). Mediation (bootstrap): COLES indirect via SELF b=0.078 (p<.001, 95% CI [0.042, 0.114]); EXCH indirect via SELF not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for England/UK, the study leveraged professional collaboration (COLES) and teacher self-efficacy (SELF) to predict classroom assessment (ASS), finding that professional collaboration had a positive direct association while exchange/co-ordination was not significant. Mediation analysis showed that professional collaboration also had significant indirect effects on classroom assessment through teacher self-efficacy. This indicates that professional collaboration may support more formative assessment practices by strengthening teachers’ efficacy beliefs, suggesting that teacher development initiatives should emphasize deeper, lesson-focused collaboration rather than only coordination-based exchanges, while recognizing the study’s correlational design.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data from 3,976 lower-secondary teachers in China and 2,376 in England/UK to examine how teacher collaboration relates to teaching practices, with teacher self-efficacy as a mediator. The authors estimate confirmatory factor models and a structural equation model in Mplus using maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors, and they test mediation via bootstrap confidence intervals. Across both countries, teacher self-efficacy shows strong positive associations with all three teaching-practice subscales (clarity of instruction, cognitive activation, and classroom assessment). Direct effects differ by collaboration form and country: exchange/co-ordination is positively related to clarity of instruction in both countries, while professional collaboration is significant for cognitive activation and classroom assessment in England but not directly significant for any teaching-practice subscale in China. The evidence is correlational (SEM mediation) and the manuscript does not report a missing-data handling strategy or any TALIS sampling-weight application in the provided text.
